title: Medical Facts for Pilots
description: Key aeromedical concepts from AIM Chapter 8 covering hypoxia, disorientation, vision, and fitness for flight

cards.back:
I - Illness (Am I sick?)
M - Medication (Am I taking any?)
S - Stress (Am I under pressure?)
A - Alcohol (8 hours, 0.04%?)
F - Fatigue (Am I rested?)
E - Eating/Emotion (Proper nutrition? Emotionally fit?)

Use BEFORE EVERY FLIGHT!

Early:
• Headache, drowsiness
• Impaired judgment
• Euphoria or belligerence
• Tingling sensations

Advanced:
• Tunnel vision
• Blue fingernails (cyanosis)
• Loss of coordination
• Unconsciousness

Symptoms vary by individual - learn yours in chamber!

5,000': Night vision deteriorates

10,000': Supplemental O2 recommended for safety

12,000'-15,000': Judgment/coordination impaired

15,000'+: Performance severely degraded, tunnel vision

18,000'-20,000': Incapacitation in 20-30 min

25,000'+: Time of useful consciousness <5 min

Flight crew:
• Above 12,500' MSL over 30 min: Required
• Above 14,000' MSL: Required entire time
• Above 15,000' MSL: Passengers must be provided

Class A (above 18,000'):
• Required at all times

Recommended: Above 10,000' day, 5,000' night

Cause: Anxiety/stress causes rapid breathing

Result: Excessive CO2 expelled

Symptoms:
• Lightheadedness
• Tingling in extremities
• Visual impairment
• Muscle spasms

Treatment:
• Slow breathing rate
• Breathe into bag
• Talk aloud (forces slower breathing)

Source: Exhaust through heater system

Properties: Colorless, odorless, tasteless

Symptoms: Headache, drowsiness, dizziness (like hypoxia)

Action:
1. Heater OFF
2. Vents/windows OPEN
3. Use O2 if available
4. Land ASAP
5. Seek medical attention

THE LEANS: Gradual bank undetected; correction feels like banking opposite way

GRAVEYARD SPIRAL: Altitude loss in turn feels like descent with wings level

SOMATOGRAVIC: Acceleration feels like pitch up

INVERSION: Level-off from climb feels like tumbling backward

CORIOLIS: Head movement in turn causes tumbling sensation

• Trust instruments, not body sensations
• Maintain instrument scan
• Avoid sudden head movements in turns
• Maintain instrument currency
• Get instrument training even if VFR only
• If disoriented, focus on attitude indicator

Statistics: Disorientation is fatal 90%+ of time

RUNWAY WIDTH:
• Narrower = appears farther (fly too low)
• Wider = appears closer (fly too high)

RUNWAY SLOPE:
• Upslope = appears closer (fly too low)
• Downslope = appears farther (fly too high)

FEATURELESS TERRAIN:
• 'Black hole' approach
• Tend to fly too low

Always use VASI/PAPI!

Dark adaptation:
• 30 minutes for full adaptation
• 20 minutes moderate with dim red light

Impaired by:
• Bright light exposure
• Smoking
• Carbon monoxide
• Altitude >5,000'
• Vitamin A deficiency

Tip: Close one eye if using bright light

Technique:
• Short, regularly spaced eye movements
• Stop briefly (1-2 seconds) at each segment
• Cover entire visible sky
• Focus at varying distances

Why stops matter:
• Eye detects motion in periphery
• But must FOCUS to see stationary targets
• A collision course aircraft has NO relative motion!

Danger signs:
• No apparent motion in windscreen
• Target appears stationary but grows larger
• Stays in same position relative to horizon

Action:
• Immediate evasive maneuver
• Watch during and after maneuver
• Report near-miss

High-risk areas: VORs, airports, airways

Regulations (14 CFR 91.17):
• 8 hours bottle to throttle
• Blood alcohol <0.04%
• Not under the influence

Facts:
• Effects amplified at altitude
• Impairs judgment and coordination
• Even small amounts affect performance
• Hangover symptoms = still impaired

Problematic medications:
• Antihistamines (drowsiness)
• Tranquilizers, sedatives
• Pain medications
• Blood pressure meds
• Diet pills
• Decongestants

Rule: If in doubt, consult AME

OTC meds can be just as dangerous as prescription!

ACUTE FATIGUE:
• Short-term, normal
• Rest restores performance

CHRONIC FATIGUE:
• Accumulated over time
• Requires extended rest
• May indicate illness

Effects:
• Slow reactions
• Poor judgment
• Reduced attention
• Fixation on tasks

Wait before flying above 8,000':

• Non-decompression dives: 12 hours minimum
• Decompression dives: 24 hours minimum
• Any dive requiring controlled ascent: 24 hours

Risk: Nitrogen bubbles in blood/tissues

Symptoms: Joint pain, numbness, paralysis

POSITIVE G (pull up):
• Blood forced to feet
• Gray-out → tunnel vision → blackout → G-LOC

NEGATIVE G (push over):
• Blood forced to head
• Red-out, headache, discomfort

Prevention:
• Anti-G straining maneuver
• Physical conditioning
• Gradual G onset

Types:
• Acute (situational, short-term)
• Chronic (ongoing life issues)

Effects:
• Reduced attention
• Impaired decision making
• Tunnel vision
• Increased errors

Management:
• Recognize signs
• Use checklists
• Reduce workload
• Consider not flying

MIDDLE EAR:
• Pressure changes during climb/descent
• Blocked by congestion = pain, hearing loss
• Valsalva maneuver to equalize

Do NOT fly with:
• Cold or sinus infection
• Ear infection
• Recent ear surgery

Descend slowly if ear block occurs

Sinuses must equalize with ambient pressure

Blocked sinuses (cold, allergies):
• Severe pain during descent
• Can cause vertigo
• May require climb back up

Prevention:
• Don't fly congested
• Use decongestant (if AME approved)
• Descend slowly

Cause: Conflict between visual and vestibular input

Symptoms:
• Nausea, sweating, pallor
• Progresses if not addressed

Prevention/Treatment:
• Fresh air
• Focus on horizon or instruments
• Avoid reading
• Medication (if approved)
• Take control if possible

Recommended characteristics:
• Block 85% visible light
• Neutral gray (true color perception)
• No image distortion
• Non-polarized for LCD displays

Why important:
• Reduce glare
• Protect eyes from UV
• Reduce fatigue
• Preserve dark adaptation

Classes:
• First Class: ATP privileges (6-12 months)
• Second Class: Commercial (12 months)
• Third Class: Private (24-60 months depending on age)

BasicMed:
• Alternative to Third Class
• Requires medical within 10 years
• Online course every 24 months
• Restrictions apply

Don't fly with:
• Fever
• Cold or flu symptoms
• Ear or sinus infection
• Recent surgery
• Severe headache
• Stomach upset

Even minor illness impairs:
• Judgment
• Reaction time
• Attention
• Coordination

When in doubt, DON'T!

Situation:
• Coordinated turn goes unnoticed
• Vestibular system adapts
• Pilot feels level

Indicators:
• Airspeed increasing
• Altitude decreasing
• Turn coordinator shows bank

Danger:
• Pulling back tightens spiral
• Can lead to structural failure or CFIT

Recovery: Trust instruments, level wings FIRST

Illusion: Stationary light appears to move

Cause: Staring at single light in darkness

Risk: Following 'moving' light into unusual attitude

Prevention:
• Avoid fixating on single light
• Maintain instrument scan
• Reference multiple points
• Trust instruments

Cause: Mistaking sloping cloud deck, lights, or stars for horizon

Result: Flying at unusual attitude while appearing level

Common situations:
• Night flight over water
• Scattered lights below
• Sloping cloud bank

Prevention: Trust instruments

Cause: Flickering light at certain frequencies (4-20 Hz)

Sources:
• Helicopter rotor
• Propeller in sun
• Strobe lights

Effects:
• Nausea, disorientation
• Seizure in susceptible individuals
• Unconsciousness (rare)

Prevention: Avoid prolonged exposure, change position

Before flying:
• Eat regular, balanced meals
• Avoid heavy, greasy foods
• Stay hydrated (especially at altitude)
• Avoid excessive caffeine

Altitude effects:
• Dehydration accelerated
• Dry cabin air
• Reduced appetite

Tip: Bring water and snacks for longer flights

At altitude without supplemental oxygen:

25,000': 3-5 minutes
30,000': 1-2 minutes
35,000': 30-60 seconds
40,000': 15-20 seconds
43,000': 9-12 seconds

Note: Times are LESS with physical activity
Rapid decompression: TUC reduced by 50%
